cards.back: $\log_b (mn) = \log_b m + \log_b n$. The log of a product equals the sum of the logs.
$\log_b \left( \frac{m}{n} \right) = \log_b m - \log_b n$. The log of a quotient equals the difference of the logs.
$\log_b (m^n) = n \log_b m$. The log of a power equals the exponent times the log of the base.

cards.front: What does it mean to [[kw:expand]] a logarithmic expression?
cards.back: To rewrite a single logarithm as a sum, difference, or product of simpler logarithms using the Product, Quotient, and Power Properties.

cards.front: What does it mean to [[kw:condense]] a logarithmic expression?
cards.back: To combine multiple logarithmic terms into a single logarithm by using the properties in reverse: Power, then Product, then Quotient.
$\log_c a = \frac{\log_b a}{\log_b c}$. With common logs: $\log_c a = \frac{\log a}{\log c}$; with natural logs: $\log_c a = \frac{\ln a}{\ln c}$.

cards.front: Why is the Change-of-Base Formula useful?
cards.back: Calculators typically only have keys for common log (base 10) and natural log (base $e$). The formula allows evaluating any logarithm using these keys.
When intensity changes, log properties simplify the difference. For doubling intensity, $L(2I) - L(I) = 10 \log 2$, a constant increase of about 3 dB.
cards.front: How does the decibel formula $L(I) = 10 \log \frac{I}{I_0}$ use log properties?
What common mistake is made when applying the Product Property?
cards.back: Thinking $\log_b(m + n) = \log_b m + \log_b n$. The property only works for multiplication inside the log, not addition.
